front.title: Upper vs. lower airway
front.summary: Why the airway is described in two halves.

back.body: The airway is split into an upper and a lower section at a named landmark. Each half has its own characteristic set of problems, which is what makes the split worth knowing rather than trivia.
back.why_it_matters: Structure names from one half are the standard distractors for the other.

front.title: Pediatric airway differences
front.summary: A child is not a small adult.

back.body: Several parts of a child's airway are proportioned differently from an adult's. Each difference changes something you physically do — how you position, how you size equipment, how you ventilate.
back.why_it_matters: It is why pediatric airway questions have different right answers than the adult versions.

back.body: In an unresponsive patient the tongue is the most likely obstruction. This maneuver moves the jaw, and the tongue with it, off the back of the throat. It is the first choice when nothing about the mechanism raises a spinal concern.
back.why_it_matters: Its one contraindication is the entire reason the other maneuver exists.

back.body: Both open the airway. Head-tilt/chin-lift is the default when nothing about the mechanism suggests a spinal injury. Jaw-thrust is for when it does — it gets the jaw forward without the head movement the default requires.
back.why_it_matters: Pick the maneuver that matches how the patient got hurt.

front.title: Non-rebreather mask
front.summary: The high-flow device for a patient still breathing on their own.

back.body: The reservoir fills while the patient exhales, so the next breath comes mostly from the bag rather than from room air. The reservoir has to be prepared before the mask goes on the face.
back.why_it_matters: Using it on a patient who is not moving enough air is the classic error — that patient needs assisted ventilation.
